title: Transistors Changed Everything. Here’s How They Work
gist: A physics explainer tracing the switching-device lineage from the 1835 electric relay through the ~1905 vacuum tube to the 1947 Bell Labs transistor, arguing each step solved a specific limitation of the last: mechanical speed, then power/fragility/size. It closes on the scale of the payoff — early transistor radios held six to 10 transistors, the iPhone 17 Pro holds up to 30 billion.

insights.claim: The transistor's evolutionary trail begins with the electric relay invented in 1835, whose core idea — using one electric current to switch a second current — is the reusable principle underlying every later switching device.
insights.so_what: The invariant across 190 years of computing hardware is current-controls-current; new device physics gets judged against that same function.
insights.quote: the idea of using a current to turn on another current opened up all kinds of possibilities
insights.locator: Of course, the telegraph used a buzzer instead of a light
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Relays existed because long telegraph wires had enough resistance to degrade signals, so splitting a 50-mile run into two 25-mile circuits joined by a relay let a second battery regenerate the pattern — an early repeater architecture.
insights.so_what: Signal regeneration to defeat distance-dependent loss is the same constraint that shapes modern interconnect and networking design.
insights.quote: The solution? Split the circuit into two 25-mile lengths and connect them with a relay.
insights.locator: But there was a problem: The longer the wire
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Relays remain widely used today, notably in cars where low-power dashboard controls switch high-power circuits for starters, headlights and air conditioners.
insights.so_what: Older switching technology does not disappear when superseded; it settles into the power-handling niches semiconductors do not serve well.
insights.locator: Anyway, relays are still widely used today
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: The vacuum tube, invented around 1905, differed from the relay in two decisive ways: no mechanical contact so output could change much faster, and continuously variable output rather than binary on/off.
insights.so_what: Speed and analog gain are separate capability axes; a device that adds both at once is what unlocks a new industry.
insights.quote: First, there's no mechanical contact, which means the output current can change much faster. Second, the output current is not just on or off; it can vary with the strength of the control voltage.
insights.locator: So this is again a current switch
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Variable output is what made the first audio amplifiers possible: feeding a weak radio signal into a vacuum tube's control voltage produced a much stronger output that preserved the original signal pattern.
insights.so_what: Amplification with fidelity — not switching — was the first commercial application; the same distinction separates analog and digital device markets today.
insights.locator: This is what made the first audio amplifiers possible
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Early computers were built as arrays of vacuum tubes controlling other vacuum tubes to form logic gates, using 1-volt and 0-volt input signals to implement AND and OR functions.
insights.so_what: Logic-gate architecture predates the transistor; the transistor changed the economics of the same architecture, not the architecture itself.
insights.locator: But wait! There's something else you could do with vacuum tubes
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Computers could have been built entirely from relays, but relays were far slower than vacuum tubes and mechanically noisy — silent, purely electronic components with no moving parts were the actual game changer.
insights.so_what: The winning technology was not the one that made computing possible but the one that made it fast and tolerable — a recurring pattern in hardware adoption.
insights.quote: Vacuum tubes were silent, purely electronic components, with no moving parts, and that was a game changer.
insights.locator: Actually, you could have built a computer with electric relays
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Vacuum tubes had three fatal problems that transistors solved simultaneously: high power draw making early computers hot and expensive to run, fragility requiring full-time crews to locate and replace dead tubes, and physical size that made machines like 1945's ENIAC fill entire rooms.
insights.so_what: Power, reliability and density are still the three axes on which compute hardware competes — the same triad that decided the 1947 transition.
insights.quote: They used a lot of power, so early computers ran hot, required massive cooling systems, and were insanely expensive to operate.
insights.locator: Still, there were three problems with vacuum tubes
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, worked by exploiting semiconductors — materials like silicon that can switch between conducting and insulating, unlike fixed conductors such as copper or insulators such as rubber.
insights.so_what: The definitional property of a semiconductor — switchable conductivity — is what any competing material system has to reproduce.
insights.quote: a semiconductor (like silicon) can switch between being one or the other
insights.locator: The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Adding extra electrons to silicon yields an n-type semiconductor and removing them yields a p-type, where the missing electrons behave as positive charges called electron holes.
insights.so_what: Doping is the fundamental controllable variable in chip fabrication; everything downstream in process technology manipulates it.
insights.quote: If you add extra electrons to silicon, you get an n-type semiconductor; take away electrons and you get a p-type.
insights.locator: There are two types of semiconductor
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: In an NPN transistor two n-type regions separated by a p-type block electron flow from source to drain until a voltage applied to the gate lets electrons move — the same current-controls-current switch as a relay, but with much finer control.
insights.so_what: Gate control is the mechanism; understanding it is what makes gate-oxide scaling and leakage-current problems legible as investment risks.
insights.quote: Yes, once again, it's basically a switch, where one current turns on a second current—but now with much finer control.
insights.locator: The two n-type semiconductors are separated by a p-type
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Transistor radios carried by teens in the 1950s and '60s contained six to 10 transistors, while the iPhone 17 Pro contains up to 30 billion — roughly a billionfold increase in device count per consumer product.
insights.so_what: The cleanest available yardstick for compounding semiconductor density; useful for calibrating claims about how much further scaling can go.
insights.quote: They contained six to 10 transistors. Today, the iPhone 17 Pro contains up to 30 billion transistors.
insights.locator: Best of all, they could be miniaturized
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: The author frames the transistor as arguably the most important invention of the 20th century, arguing that without it there would be no personal computers or cell phones and therefore no Amazon, video games, dating apps, streaming, social media, Apple Pay, Google Maps or AI.
insights.so_what: A reminder that today's software and AI valuations rest on one physical device class whose scaling limits are a systemic risk factor.
insights.quote: it's maybe only the most important invention of the 20th century
insights.locator: But the transistor deserves its own headline
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain

insights.claim: Transistors are pervasive well beyond computing devices — cars alone contain billions of them.
insights.so_what: Auto content per vehicle is a large and often underweighted slice of semiconductor end demand.
insights.locator: Life would be completely different without transistors
insights.speaker: Rhett Allain
